claims.text: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi will exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition across a broad temperature window.
The transition is primarily enabled by a single-phase solid solution that resists localized embrittling segregation.
CrMnFeCoNi maintains ductile failure mechanisms in temperature ranges where conventional alloys suffer temper embrittlement.
The proposed alloy is equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
The initial CrMnFeCoNi material is as-cast and solutionized.
The initial CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a single-phase face-centered-cubic structure.
The initial alloy has grain sizes in the micrometer range.
Mechanical behavior will be tested over temperatures from approximately −150 °C to 600 °C.
A controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation or surface embrittlement during heating.
The alloy has suppressed grain-boundary segregation.
The alloy retains a stable single-phase structure over the tested conditions.
Suppressed segregation and single-phase stability reduce the formation of brittle precipitates or secondary phases.
High configurational entropy and uniform element distribution reduce the driving force for phase separation and precipitation.
Reduced phase separation and precipitation minimize embrittling grain-boundary effects.
The proposed mechanism preserves ductile dislocation- and twinning-mediated deformation.
CrMnFeCoNi will retain higher overall ductility than conventional low-alloy steels across the tested temperature range.
CrMnFeCoNi will show a mild ductility decrease at intermediate temperatures followed by ductility recovery at higher temperatures.
Conventional low- and medium-alloy steels often undergo severe temper embrittlement over a narrow temperature range, producing abrupt ductility loss.
Secondary phases introduced by contamination or improper processing may compromise single-phase stability and reduce ductility.
Transition temperatures may vary with composition, processing parameters, and grain size.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the behavior a ductile–brittle–ductile transition, but the predicted outcome specifies only a mild intermediate ductility decrease while emphasizing retention of ductility. It does not clearly predict a genuinely brittle intermediate regime.
